items.text: Pause semantics (chosen 2026-11-04): `resume` clears the paused flag. If `next_run` passed while the job was paused, it reschedules from now instead of firing immediately, which matches how `run_pending` treats missed runs. Paused jobs are excluded from `next_run` and `idle_seconds`, so a stale `next_run` cannot make `idle_seconds` negative and cause a busy sleep loop. `run_all` still runs paused jobs as an explicit override, because only `run_pending` should skip them. Pausing or resuming an unknown tag is a silent no-op.

items.text: Convention (decided 2026-11-04): new APIs are added only on `Scheduler`, with no new module-level shortcuts, because the project is moving everyone off the global default scheduler. For example, `Scheduler.get_jobs_for(func)` was first added together with a module-level `schedule.get_jobs_for(func)`, but the module-level version was removed, so the Scheduler method is the only entry point. Later the same day, `pause(tag)` and `resume(tag)` were implemented on both `Scheduler` and the module-level default scheduler. That departs from this rule, and the sources do not say whether the rule was deliberately revised or the departure was an oversight, so it is unresolved.

items.text: `Scheduler.get_jobs_for(func)` (added 2026-11-04) returns all scheduled jobs running `func` regardless of arguments. It compares against the original function passed to `.do()` and skips jobs with no `.do()` call yet. It lets users cancel by function without holding Job objects: `for job in scheduler.get_jobs_for(f): scheduler.cancel_job(job)`. It is deliberately implemented only on `Scheduler`, with no module-level shortcut. It was committed on branch `feature/jobs-by-func` as `ffcd71c`, not pushed, with no PR opened. Its test `test_get_jobs_for` in test_schedule.py builds its own `Scheduler()` rather than using the global default (82 tests passed). `docs/reference.rst` lists only module-level functions, so no docs entry was added for this method.

items.text: Timezone support and correctness has been a major recurring theme: timezone support for .at() was added (#517), followed by repeated fixes (#583), more timezone tests (#602), pytz documented as a dependency for timezones (#601), improved timezone handling in next_run (#604), and further bugfixes (#623), between April 2022 and May 2024, because schedules were off when using .at with timezone.

The at() method of the schedule library was extended in January 2019 (Nathan Wailes) to support seconds-level scheduling: it accepts timestamps with 1 second precision, supports recurring tasks like every().minute.at(':30') (initially via a '::30' syntax that was later removed, with READMEs updated), and the at(':SS') bug was fixed. It validates the format based on the selected units, rejects whitespace, and raises an exception for non-string or wrongly formatted input.

Project released versions 0.3.0 (June 2014): CI switched to test against Python 3.4 instead of 3.3 (4738891), version bumped to 0.3.0 (fffe355), READMEs updated for 0.3.0 (a3ff9e5), and a downloads badge added to README.rst (47fcf1d). | When: 2014-06-13 to 2014-06-14 | Involving: Daniel Bader
